challenges.name: retry-everything-quiz
challenges.title: Which export failures are worth a retry?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the export worker: the log of an export retried ten times, and a first attempt at classifying errors.

questions.question:
Export worker log (10 attempts, exponential backoff from 1 s, capped at 30 s):

14:03:02.118 exp-7731 attempt=1 HttpError: reports API answered 404 (course "nestjs-basics")
14:03:03.121 exp-7731 attempt=2 HttpError: reports API answered 404 (course "nestjs-basics")
14:03:05.125 exp-7731 attempt=3 HttpError: reports API answered 404 (course "nestjs-basics")
   ... attempts 4 to 9: the same 404 ...
14:05:33.161 exp-7731 attempt=10 HttpError: reports API answered 404 (course "nestjs-basics")
14:05:33.163 exp-7731 ALERT export exp-7731 failed

The course nestjs-basics was renamed months ago; GET /courses/nestjs-basics/progress answers 404 every time.

Statement: "None of the nine retries could have succeeded, and the alert came about two and a half minutes later than it could have."
questions.explanation: True. A 404 for a course that does not exist describes the request, not a temporary state of the reports API: sending the same request again gets the same answer, so every retry was wasted work and the worker was blocked for 151 seconds (1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 30 x 4 seconds of sleeping). The alert could have been sent after the first attempt at 14:03:02 instead of at 14:05:33. A 404 is a permanent error: fail the export at once with the reason and alert. The misconception is that more attempts always make a worker more reliable; for permanent errors they only add load and delay the moment someone finds out.

False. The first half is accurate - the code treats 429 like any other 4xx and stops - but that outcome is wrong. 429 does not say the request is invalid; it says the client is sending too many requests right now, and Retry-After: 5 says when to try again. The same request will very likely succeed after five seconds, so it is retryable, and so is 408 Request Timeout. The correct rule is 4xx except 408 and 429 is permanent; 5xx, timeouts and connection resets are retryable. The misconception is that the status class alone decides; the meaning of the specific code does.

challenges.name: spot-the-ai-mistake-retry-everything
challenges.title: Spot the AI Mistake: retrying errors that can never succeed
challenges.description: An AI assistant was asked: "The course export worker fails now and then and instructors have to click Export again. Make the export worker reliable." It wrapped the export in runExportJob: up to 10 attempts with exponential backoff (1 s doubling, capped at 30 s) that honours Retry-After, then an alert. Its tests, with a reports API that times out or answers 503 or 429 and then recovers, passed. In production the export queue falls behind and alerts arrive minutes late: an export with a malformed course id, a 404 or 403 from the reports API, or a missing template file is attempted 10 times over 151 seconds before the alert. Fix runExportJob so that only errors that can go away on their own are retried: TimeoutError, a connection reset (code "ECONNRESET"), HttpError 5xx, 408 and 429 (waiting retryAfterMs when set). ValidationError, HttpError 4xx other than 408 and 429, and a missing file (code "ENOENT") are permanent: fail the job at once, without sleeping and without another attempt, and alert immediately. Keep the limit, the backoff, the alert and the result as they are. Input: a list of export jobs { id, courseId, format, script }, where script lists what each attempt meets ("ok", "reports:timeout", "reports:reset", "reports:<status>[:<retryAfterSeconds>]", "template:missing", "storage:timeout", "storage:<status>"; the last entry repeats). Output: one line per job with its status, attempts, fake worker time and alert time, then a total line. The public tests pass on the assistant's code; the hidden tests use failures that never recover.
hints: Inside the catch block, before deciding to sleep, what question about the error should the worker ask, and what does it do today with an error whose answer can never change?

Look at the line that decides whether the loop ends early, and at the information each error carries: its class (ValidationError, TimeoutError, HttpError), the status of an HttpError, and the code of a system error. The decision has to happen before the sleep, or a permanent error still costs one backoff delay.

A similar decision for an SMTP mailer, where the rule is reversed: reply codes 4xx are temporary and 5xx are permanent. With attempts that meet 451, then 451, then 250, the mail is sent on attempt 3 after two backoff delays; with 550 on the first attempt, the job fails on attempt 1 with no delay and the alert goes out at once. Write the rule as one small function that takes the error and returns whether the same request could succeed later.
